linkedin.headline: 3x Amazon SDE Intern | Backend, AI, Data & Product Engineer | Building Reliable Systems
linkedin.about:
I build backend systems, data workflows, developer tools, and AI-enabled products that turn ambiguous problems into usable software.

I completed three Amazon SDE internship terms across Ads and FinTech/business-systems environments, and I have led client-facing product delivery through Forward Automations. My current work spans Tenure, split AI runtimes for evaluation, context, and workflow leverage, macOS developer tools, basketball/data products, and applied AI systems.

I am especially interested in backend engineering, applied AI, data engineering, platform/developer tools, product engineering, and solutions or forward-deployed roles.

Selected work: https://jakye.netlify.app/
GitHub: https://github.com/jakyeamos

backlog.title: Why institutional knowledge disappears before organizations realize it
backlog.hook: The hard part of employee transition is not writing a document after the fact; it is capturing the tacit decisions while the work is happening.
backlog.context: When someone leaves, the document they leave behind usually records the procedure, not the judgment that made the procedure work.
backlog.personalAngle: That gap is what pushed me toward Tenure, a LaunchNY cohort venture for turning specialist knowledge into reviewed, cited, permissioned internal knowledge.
backlog.nextStep: I’m working through the capture flow first, because a useful answer should still show where it came from and who signed off on it.

backlog.title: Why Tenure puts human review between extraction and organizational truth
backlog.hook: An AI extraction pipeline is only useful if the organization can see what was extracted, why it was extracted, and who approved it.
backlog.context: The dangerous step in an AI knowledge system is the quiet jump from extracted text to organizational truth.
backlog.personalAngle: Tenure keeps a human review step between those two things so people can see what was captured, why it was captured, and what is still uncertain.
backlog.nextStep: The next test is making that review feel like part of the work instead of another queue nobody wants to own.

backlog.title: The boundary Tenure refuses to cross
backlog.hook: Tenure is not a transcript summarizer and it is not allowed to turn ungrounded model output into client knowledge.
backlog.context: A polished transcript can look authoritative even when it has missed the decision that mattered.
backlog.personalAngle: Tenure is not meant to turn a model summary into knowledge just because the prose sounds confident.
backlog.nextStep: The product is pilot-ready, but the review and citation boundaries are still the part I’m treating as core product work.

backlog.title: Tenure in 90 seconds: capture to reviewed knowledge
backlog.hook: A short walkthrough of the capture, extraction, review, wiki, and cited-Q&A loop.
backlog.context: The Tenure loop is meant to follow a piece of work from capture to something another person can actually use.
backlog.personalAngle: I want the product to make the handoff visible: capture, extraction, review, wiki, then cited questions and answers.
backlog.nextStep: The demo should show the working path and the places where a person still has to make the call.

backlog.title: AI-assisted engineering needs operational context, not just better prompts
backlog.hook: The useful question is not what an agent generated; it is what evidence, constraints, and handoffs shaped the work.
backlog.context: When AI-assisted engineering goes wrong, the missing ingredient is often not another prompt; it is the context around the task.
backlog.personalAngle: AIOS grew out of wanting receipts for the evidence, constraints, and handoffs that shaped a change.
backlog.nextStep: I’m still modernizing the local-first system, so the useful thing to show is the context packet and what it preserves.

backlog.title: Why quality checks should produce evidence before they produce edits
backlog.hook: Quality Runner is intentionally read-only: the first artifact is a reviewable finding and remediation plan, not an automatic source change.
backlog.context: A quality tool that edits the source before anyone can inspect the reasoning makes review harder, not easier.
backlog.personalAngle: Quality Runner starts with a finding and an ordered remediation plan because I want the evidence to be readable before a change is proposed.
backlog.nextStep: The published package is the proof surface; the next work is making the read-only workflow useful across more repositories.

backlog.title: The engineering workflow I wanted before opening a pull request
backlog.hook: Changed-line coverage is easier to fix before review than after a pull request turns it into a social negotiation.
backlog.context: By the time a pull request tells you a changed line has no useful test coverage, the conversation has already become more expensive.
backlog.personalAngle: Pre-CR Suite is my attempt to move that check to the moment before review, while the change is still local and explainable.
backlog.nextStep: The interesting engineering work is keeping the check useful across editors without making the developer learn a new workflow.

backlog.title: Quality Runner in 90 seconds
backlog.hook: Show the CLI discovering checks, producing evidence-backed findings, and writing an ordered remediation artifact.
backlog.context: I wanted a quality workflow that could show its work before it suggested a fix.
backlog.personalAngle: In this short demo, Quality Runner discovers checks, records evidence-backed findings, and writes a remediation artifact without changing source code.
backlog.nextStep: The current surface is intentionally read-only; the next step is to keep that review boundary useful as the checks get more capable.

backlog.title: Sports analytics should show uncertainty, not just rankings
backlog.hook: The interesting question is not whether a metric is high; it is how much evidence it takes before the metric becomes decision-useful.
backlog.context: A basketball metric can look precise long before there is enough evidence to make it useful.
backlog.personalAngle: BBDSE/CourtIQ is where I’ve been testing how to put uncertainty and role context next to the number instead of hiding them behind a ranking.
backlog.nextStep: The public deployment is paused, but the reliability work is still the part I trust enough to keep showing.

backlog.title: What Signal Lab measures before it recommends a basketball metric
backlog.hook: Before building a dashboard around a stat, I want to know how quickly it stabilizes, where it gets noisy, and how role changes affect it.
backlog.context: Before I put a basketball stat into a decision surface, I want to know how quickly it stabilizes and where it gets noisy.
backlog.personalAngle: Signal Lab exists for that unglamorous step: sample-size analysis, stability curves, shrinkage, and role/context splits.
backlog.nextStep: The work is still research rather than a production analytics platform, which is exactly why the diagnostics matter.

backlog.title: Why CourtIQ and BBDSE belong in the same product lane
backlog.hook: The analytics layer is more useful when it reaches a decision-training surface instead of stopping at a report.
backlog.context: A report can answer a question and still leave the person looking at it with no next move.
backlog.personalAngle: CourtIQ and BBDSE belong together because the analytics can become a decision-training surface instead of ending at a chart.
backlog.nextStep: I’m keeping the product claim narrow while the suite is still being shaped and the public deployment is paused.

backlog.title: BBDSE/CourtIQ in 90 seconds
backlog.hook: Walk through the decision surface, the analytics boundary, and what remains paused or under development.
backlog.context: The most useful basketball product surface is not the ranking by itself; it is the decision a person can make with the evidence around it.
backlog.personalAngle: This walkthrough connects the BBDSE analytics boundary to CourtIQ’s training surface and shows what is actually working.
backlog.nextStep: I’ll also show what remains paused, because that is part of the current state rather than a footnote.

backlog.title: What makes a government-contracting workflow useful to a small firm
backlog.hook: The product has to connect RFP analysis, proposal work, procurement intelligence, and reviewed follow-up without exposing tenant data.
backlog.context: Small firms do not need another isolated RFP summary; they need the analysis to survive the handoff into proposal work.
backlog.personalAngle: BidCamp connects RFP analysis, procurement intelligence, and reviewed follow-up in a multi-tenant workflow without making tenant data part of the demo.
backlog.nextStep: It is live in closed beta, so I’m showing the workflow and keeping adoption claims out of the story.

backlog.title: The common thread in my client work
backlog.hook: Across healthcare, architecture, live-event software, and marketing systems, the recurring job has been turning an ambiguous workflow into something usable under a short deadline.
backlog.context: The client work has looked different on the surface - healthcare, architecture, live events, and marketing - but the underlying problem is usually the same: a messy workflow with a short deadline.
backlog.personalAngle: At Forward Automations, I’ve worked as a CTO turning those ambiguous requests into usable products and internal systems.
backlog.nextStep: I can share the patterns and anonymized outcomes; private repositories, customer data, and client-sensitive details stay private.

backlog.title: Why legal-time software needs explicit decision-support boundaries
backlog.hook: A calculation can be useful without pretending to be legal advice; the product has to make that boundary visible.
backlog.context: Time calculations in legal workflows are consequential partly because a small misunderstanding can change what someone thinks happens next.
backlog.personalAngle: CrimClock is a legal-time intelligence platform, so the product has to explain the calculation without pretending to be legal advice.
backlog.nextStep: The reviewer preview is where I’m testing whether the boundary is clear in the interface, not just in a disclaimer.

backlog.title: From room photo to renovation visualization
backlog.hook: A short walkthrough of the working vision, transformation, and rough-estimation path, including the flows that are not finished yet.
backlog.context: A room photo can start a useful renovation conversation, but turning it into a trustworthy estimate takes more than a generated image.
backlog.personalAngle: RemodelVision connects a working vision/transformation path to rough estimation while keeping the incomplete product flows visible.
backlog.nextStep: The current pipeline is real and useful to inspect; persistence and other product flows are still unfinished.
